identity.title: One Order or Two Dimensions?
identity.description: A recipe's steps and a pricing comparison can look similarly laid out on a page — but they're structurally nothing alike. One is a sequence. The other is a grid of relationships. This lesson builds the model for telling them apart and choosing the HTML that actually matches.

primaryCapability.statement: Distinguish genuinely sequential information from tabular, two-dimensional relationships, and model each with the HTML structure that actually matches it.

knows: HTML is a tree of nested elements
Heading levels represent an outline, not font size
canDo: Read and construct correctly nested markup
likelyMisconceptions: A table is just a way to make things line up visually
Any list of items should be a table if it needs to look organized

canDo: Identify whether a given set of information is sequential or tabular
Construct an ordered list for a sequence
Construct a table where rows and columns represent a real relationship

learning.targetMentalModel: Sequential data has one dimension — this, then this, then this — and order is the only relationship that matters. Tabular data has two dimensions: each cell's meaning depends on both its row and its column at once. The right structure follows from which of those is actually true, not from how you want it to look.

experience.startingState: The learner can nest markup and structure headings but has been treating 'looks organized' as the reason to reach for a table.
experience.narrativeContext: Two real examples — a recipe's steps and a plan comparison — are placed side by side to make the structural difference visible before it's named.
experience.primaryInteraction: Seeing the two structures compared directly, predicting which fits a new example, then constructing a real table.
experience.expectedOutcome: The learner chooses list vs. table from the shape of the data, not from how they want it to look.

activities.title: One Order or Two Dimensions?
activities.instruction: Two examples. Only one is a table.

content.title: One Order or Two Dimensions?
content.hook:
1. Preheat the oven.
2. Mix the batter.
3. Bake for 20 minutes.

Plan     Storage     Price
Basic    10GB        $5
Pro      100GB       $15

Both of these are "organized." Only one of them is actually a table.
content.context: The difference isn't how they look. It's what relationship the structure is claiming to represent.
goals: Tell sequential data apart from tabular data
Model each with the matching HTML structure

activities.title: One Dimension vs. Two
activities.instruction: The actual structural difference, side by side.

content.title: One Dimension vs. Two
content.description: The recipe steps have exactly one relationship that matters: what comes before what. That's it — one dimension. The pricing plan has two: which plan (row), and which attribute of that plan (column) — "Pro"'s storage only means something because it's in the Pro row AND the Storage column at once. That's a genuinely two-dimensional relationship, and it's what <table> exists to represent.

activities.title: Which Structure Fits?
activities.instruction: A packing list: "Passport, charger, headphones, sunscreen." There's no meaningful order and no second dimension — just items. What's the right structure?

options.text: An unordered list — items with no meaningful sequence and no row/column relationship
An ordered list — the numbering shows how many items there are
A table — it keeps the items visually aligned

hints.text: Ask whether there's a real relationship being represented, or just a set of things.
There's no before/after here, and no second dimension — just a collection of unrelated items.

activities.title: Build the Table
activities.instruction: Complete the table so it has a header row with "Plan" and "Price", and one data row: "Pro", "$15".

testCases.description: There are exactly two header cells
There are exactly two data cells
The data row's first cell reads "Pro"

hints.text: Each row is a <tr>. Header cells inside a row are <th>; data cells are <td>.
You need two <tr> elements: one with two <th>, one with two <td>.

activities.title: A New Case
activities.instruction: You're marking up a weekly class schedule: for each day, what subject is taught in each time slot. Which structure actually fits the relationship being represented?

content.scenario: A grid where each cell's meaning depends on both its day (column) and its time slot (row) at once — e.g. "Monday, 10am" means something specific and different from "Monday, 2pm" or "Tuesday, 10am".

options.text: A table — the subject in each cell genuinely depends on both its row and its column together.
A separate ordered list for each day, since each day's classes happen in order.
Nested unordered lists — days containing time slots — since it's really just categories inside categories.

content.title: What You Can Do Now
takeaways: Sequential data has one relationship that matters: order. Model it with <ol> (or <ul> when order genuinely doesn't matter).
Tabular data has two dimensions at once — a cell's meaning depends on its row AND its column together. That's what <table>/<tr>/<th>/<td> represent.
The right structure follows from the actual relationship in the data, not from how you want it to look.

requirements: table header cells use <th> so assistive technology can announce row/column context
